explainBack.question: Why does this result not prove AI rejected one graduate's applications?
explainBack.answer: The study compares groups of majors, not people: the most AI-exposed tenth of majors had about five percentage points lower employment than the least-exposed 60%, after netting out their 2022 gap. Exposure itself only estimates how much AI could help with tasks in occupations tied to a major — it counts no actual replacements. The authors cannot rule out other field-specific changes that coincided with ChatGPT, and their records miss self-employment and graduate school. So a single graduate's rejections could reflect any of these things or plain individual variation; the study measures pressure on a group, not causes of one person's outcome.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer should cite the group comparison and 2022 baseline adjustment (P004), the capability-not-replacement definition of exposure (P003), and the confounding/omission caveats (P007), while distinguishing group averages from individual diagnosis (P010, P011).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this answer: every element of the causal chain and its limits appears in P003, P004, P007 and P010, so a reader can explain back correctly in ordinary language.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A 2025 information-systems graduate spends her first year building a freelance app-development business instead of taking a salaried job. Her uncle reads this study and tells her she is 'one of the five percentage points' — proof AI pushed her out of employment.
unseenTransfer.question: Does the study's employment decline show that graduates like her were displaced by AI?
unseenTransfer.answer: No, on two grounds the article supplies. First, the study's employment records omit self-employment entirely (P007), so a working freelancer would be recorded as not employed — she may be counted in the decline without being jobless at all, and the authors flag this as a reason the employment estimate needs care. Second, the five-point figure is a group-level difference between exposure deciles after a 2022 adjustment (P004); it assigns no cause to any individual, and exposure measures capability, not actual replacement (P003). Her situation is one the data cannot classify, let alone diagnose.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct transfer requires invoking the omitted self-employment coverage (P007), the group-comparison structure (P004), and the exposure definition (P003), rather than treating the headline number as an individual displacement count.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism transfers cleanly to this new scenario absent from the text; a reader who absorbed P003, P004 and P007 can resolve it correctly, so transfer passes.

reader.summary: A disciplined, well-scoped news report: it states the September working paper's five-point employment and 13% earnings estimates with their reference group and 2022 baseline, defines exposure as capability rather than replacement, keeps points-vs-percent arithmetic honest and explicitly illustrative, preserves confounding, coverage and review limits to the end, and converts it all into one concrete career-office question while refusing to turn a group average into a personal verdict.

sample.reason: Paper (CES 26-56, September 2026) analyzes bachelor's graduates 2016–2024 from participating institutions covering 'approximately 29% of all bachelor's degrees conferred from 2016 to 2024', matching P002 exactly.

period.reason: LEHD data described as available 'for every quarter between Q1 2016 and Q3 2025', i.e., employment records through September 2025 as P002 states.

exposure.reason: Paper states the Eloundou GPT-4 Beta measure is 'based on AI's capacity to perform certain tasks, but not necessarily reflective of its actual usage', and exposure never counts realized replacements — matching P003's 'does not count jobs AI actually replaced'.

employment.reason: Regression-adjusted estimates show a five-percentage-point employment decline for the top exposure decile relative to the bottom six deciles with 2022 as reference period ('net of the difference... in calendar year 2022'), and the top decile is 'heavily dominated by computer science' — matching P004 including the 2022-difference framing.

earnings.reason: Paper reports ~thirteen percent decline in full-quarter initial earnings, measured for the dominant job two quarters post-graduation with positive earnings in preceding, current and subsequent quarters — matching P006's 'main full-quarter job... two quarters after graduation'.

causal-limit.reason: Authors argue for 'a substantial role for generative AI' but state their design 'cannot rule out other time-varying shocks to particular fields that coincide with the diffusion of generative AI' — exactly the limit retained in P007.

missing.reason: Section 7.3: 'LEHD data do not include information on self-employment, nor do they contain information on graduate school enrollment', matching P007's omission statement.

facts.summary: All nine claims — sample coverage (29%, 2016–2024), record window (Q3 2025), capability-based exposure, five-point employment decline vs the bottom six deciles with 2022 reference, ~13% full-quarter earnings decline two quarters out, unresolvable field-specific confounders, LEHD omission of self-employment and graduate school, non-representative institution sample, and the no-review/no-endorsement status — verify against the Census working paper with attribution and limits preserved; factual integrity, freshness, dated change and uncertainty handling all pass.
